title: Reading the Result: Vaccine Immunity, the Fourfold RPR Rule, Chlamydia NAAT and Rapid-Test Controls
summary: Learn which hepatitis B pattern means vaccine immunity, why a syphilis titer must change fourfold while treponemal tests stay reactive, how a positive chlamydia NAAT is acted on, and what built-in and external controls on rapid kits each check.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 58 Hits 16–19, checked against the CDC 2023 hepatitis B screening recommendations (Conners 2023), the CDC 2021 STI treatment guidelines (Workowski 2021), the CDC Ready? Set? Test! waived-testing booklet (PDF, text extracted) and 42 CFR 493.1256 and 493.15 (eCFR). Qualifications: anti-HBs can be passive after HBIG (rv-ch58-hbs-vaccine-context); a fourfold RPR fall is the threshold for a significant change, not proof of cure, and treponemal tests stay reactive in most rather than all patients (rv-ch58-rpr-fourfold-context); built-in controls check more than flow, and external controls are also due with each new shipment and new tester (rv-ch58-rapid-test-controls); the control rules are US (CDC/CLIA) and Philippine rules are not covered (rv-ch58-us-qc-rules). Not taught: Hit 22 (active surveillance), the Number Vault table.

objectives: Interpret anti-HBs, anti-HBc and HBsAg patterns to separate vaccine immunity from resolved infection.
Apply the fourfold (two-dilution) rule to nontreponemal titers and explain why treponemal tests are not used to follow treatment.
State the recommended action after a positive chlamydia NAAT, including partner management.
Distinguish what built-in and external controls on rapid kits check, and when external controls are run.

scenes.title: Four results on the serology bench
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: four items wait on the serology bench. (1) A health-care student: anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative, HBsAg negative. (2) A patient treated for primary syphilis: RPR 1:16 before treatment, 1:4 six months later; the treponemal test is still reactive. (3) An asymptomatic 22-year-old screened by NAAT: Chlamydia trachomatis positive. (4) A new lot of rapid antigen kits has arrived; the built-in control line appears on every device. Question token: “Immune? Cured? Treat? Ready?”

cues.text: Four results wait on the serology bench. A student’s hepatitis B panel: anti-HBs positive, anti-HBc negative.
A patient treated for syphilis: the RPR fell from one in sixteen to one in four, but the treponemal test is still reactive.
An asymptomatic twenty-two-year-old has a positive chlamydia NAAT.
And a new lot of rapid antigen kits shows its control line every time. Immune, cured, treat, or ready to use?

scenes.title: Which marker says what
scenes.altText: Schematic marker cards. Hepatitis B (CDC 2023): HBsAg = current infection; anti-HBs after HBsAg clears = recovery, and anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL 1–2 months after a completed vaccine series = immunity; total anti-HBc develops in all HBV infections, resolved or current, usually persists for life, and is NOT made after vaccination. Syphilis (CDC 2021): nontreponemal tests (RPR, VDRL) are reported as titers and used to monitor treatment response; most people with a reactive treponemal test stay reactive for the rest of their lives regardless of treatment, so treponemal tests are not used to follow therapy.

cues.text: Start with hepatitis B. Total anti-core antibody, anti-HBc, appears in every hepatitis B infection, current or resolved, and usually lasts for life. People whose immunity comes from the vaccine do not make anti-HBc.
Anti-HBs is the protective surface antibody. After a completed vaccine series, ten milli-international units per millilitre or more means immunity. After infection, it appears as HBsAg clears.
Now syphilis. Nontreponemal tests, the RPR and VDRL, are titrated, and the titer is what you follow after treatment.
Treponemal tests answer a different question. Most people who become treponemal-reactive stay reactive for life, even after adequate treatment, so they are not used to judge a response.

scenes.title: The rules that turn a result into an action
scenes.altText: Rule cards. HBV pattern table (CDC 2023): HBsAg −/anti-HBs +/anti-HBc − = immune, inferred from previous vaccination (reassure if series completed; complete it if partial); HBsAg −/anti-HBs +/anti-HBc + = resolved infection; HBIG gives passive anti-HBs for 4–6 months, so anti-HBs within 6 months of HBIG does not show immune status. RPR: a fourfold change (two dilutions, 1:16 → 1:4 or 1:8 → 1:32) in the same test method is needed for a clinically significant difference; one dilution is within test variation; RPR and VDRL titers cannot be compared directly. Chlamydia (CDC 2021): asymptomatic infection is common; NAAT is the most sensitive and recommended test; treat all persons with chlamydial infection promptly; refer partners from the previous 60 days for evaluation, testing and presumptive treatment.

cues.text: Hepatitis B patterns. Anti-HBs positive with anti-HBc and HBsAg negative is immunity inferred from vaccination. Anti-HBs and anti-HBc both positive is a resolved infection. One catch: hepatitis B immune globulin supplies borrowed anti-HBs for four to six months.

Syphilis titers. A meaningful change is fourfold, two dilutions, such as one in sixteen to one in four, measured with the same test method. A one-dilution change is within the test’s own variation, and RPR and VDRL titers are not compared with each other.
Chlamydia. Most infections cause no symptoms, which is why people are screened. NAAT is the most sensitive test and the recommended one, and anyone with chlamydial infection is treated promptly.
Treatment includes the partners. Sex partners from the previous sixty days are referred for evaluation, testing and presumptive treatment.

props.label: Partners, last 60 days: test and treat

scenes.title: Built-in versus external controls
scenes.altText: Two control cards (CDC Ready? Set? Test! booklet for waived testing). Internal (built-in, procedural) controls show that the test is working, the sample volume was adequate, the sample moved through the strip correctly, and instrument electronics work. External controls are materials like patient samples that check the whole testing process from sample application to interpretation; test them at least as often as the manufacturer specifies and with each new shipment, each change in lot number and each new tester. A failed control of either kind means patient results are held. US rule (42 CFR 493.1256): for non-waived qualitative tests, a negative and a positive control each day of patient testing unless an approved equivalent is used; reagent lots and shipments are checked for positive and negative reactivity. Hook answers.

cues.text: Rapid kits carry two kinds of control. The built-in control line shows that the device works, that enough sample was added, and that the sample flowed correctly along the strip.

External controls are run like patient samples, with known positive and negative material. They check the whole process, from applying the sample to reading the result. Run them with each new shipment, each new lot and each new tester, and as often as the manufacturer says.

If either kind of control fails, patient results wait. Back to the hook: the student is vaccine-immune; the syphilis titer fell fourfold, an appropriate response, and the treponemal test will likely stay reactive.
The chlamydia NAAT is treated now, with partners referred, and the new kit lot is not ready until its external positive and negative controls pass.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Anti-HBs positive means past infection” (✓ anti-HBs alone with anti-HBc negative = vaccine immunity; anti-HBc marks infection); “The FTA-ABS should turn negative after cure” (✓ most treponemal tests stay reactive for life; follow the RPR titer, fourfold = significant); “The control line appeared, so the new lot works” (✓ the built-in control does not replace external positive and negative controls for a new lot).

cues.text: Trap one: anti-HBs positive means a past infection. No: without anti-HBc it means vaccine immunity. Anti-HBc is the infection marker.
Trap two: the treponemal test should turn negative after cure. No: most stay reactive for life. Follow the RPR titer, and look for a fourfold change.
Trap three: the control line appeared, so the new lot works. No: run external positive and negative controls with each new lot.

props.title: ✗ “The treponemal test turns negative.”
lines: ✓ Usually reactive for life; follow RPR

scenes.title: Core is a scar, the line is a pulse
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Anti-HBc is a SCAR: only a real infection leaves it. RPR is a THERMOMETER: read it twice and believe only a two-step change. The treponemal test is a TATTOO: it usually stays. The built-in line is a PULSE: it shows the strip is alive, not that it sees the antigen.” Tokens: scar = anti-HBc · thermometer = RPR · tattoo = treponemal · pulse = control line. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: anti-HBc is a scar, left only by real infection. The RPR is a thermometer: trust only a two-step change. The treponemal test is a tattoo: it usually stays. And the control line is a pulse: the strip is alive, but that does not prove it sees antigen.

Where it breaks: an isolated anti-HBc can have several causes; borrowed anti-HBs from immune globulin fakes immunity for months; some people never reach a fourfold fall, and some treponemal tests do revert; and the built-in control does check sample volume and flow.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Anti-HBs + / anti-HBc − = vaccine immune · RPR fourfold, same method · treponemal usually reactive for life”, “CT NAAT + → treat + partners (60 days) · new lot → external + and − controls”.

cues.text: Anti-HBs without anti-HBc means vaccine immunity, a syphilis titer must change fourfold in the same test method to matter while the treponemal test usually stays reactive, a positive chlamydia NAAT is treated promptly along with recent partners, and a new lot of rapid kits needs external positive and negative controls because the built-in line cannot prove the whole process works.

explanation.what: Plain language: some results mean little on their own and only make sense with a partner test or a rule. A protective hepatitis B antibody without the infection antibody means the person was vaccinated. A syphilis blood titer must drop by two dilution steps to count as a real change, while the confirmatory syphilis test usually stays positive for life. A positive chlamydia NAAT is treated straight away, along with partners. A rapid kit’s own control line proves the strip ran, but known positive and negative samples are still needed to show the kit works. Scientific terms: HBsAg, anti-HBs, total anti-HBc, IgM anti-HBc, hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG), nontreponemal test (RPR, VDRL), treponemal test, fourfold titer change, serologic response, nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), presumptive partner treatment, expedited partner therapy (EPT), internal (built-in, procedural) control, external control, lot, waived test, CLIA.
explanation.why: Every hepatitis B infection, current or resolved, induces anti-HBc, but vaccine-derived immunity does not, so anti-HBc separates infection from vaccination. A one-dilution difference is within the performance of nontreponemal tests, so only a two-dilution change in the same method is treated as significant. Chlamydial infection is often silent and NAAT is very sensitive, so a positive result is treated promptly, and treating partners prevents reinfection. A built-in line shows flow and sample adequacy, but only external material checks the whole process, sample application to interpretation.
explanation.measure: HBV (CDC 2023): HBsAg −/anti-HBs +/anti-HBc − = immune, inferred from vaccination (≥10 mIU/mL after a completed series); HBsAg −/anti-HBs +/anti-HBc + = resolved infection; anti-HBs within 6 months of HBIG does not show immune status. Syphilis (CDC 2021): fourfold = two dilutions (1:16 → 1:4); same test method, preferably same laboratory; failure to fall fourfold within 12 months of primary or secondary syphilis treatment may mean failure, but 10–20% of adequately treated people do not reach it. Chlamydia: NAAT recommended; treat promptly; partners from the previous 60 days; no test of cure in nonpregnant persons on recommended regimens; retest at 3 months. Rapid kits (CDC booklet): external controls at least as often as the manufacturer says and with each new shipment, lot change and new tester.
explanation.differs: Vaccine immunity (anti-HBc −) vs resolved infection (anti-HBc +); nontreponemal titer (follows treatment) vs treponemal test (usually stays reactive); one-dilution change (noise) vs fourfold change (significant); built-in control (device, volume, flow) vs external controls (whole process).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the serologic pattern of vaccine immunity, decide whether an RPR change is significant, choose the next step after a positive chlamydia NAAT, or explain why external controls are run on a new lot of rapid kits.

questions.stem: A health-care student’s screening panel shows HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive (above 10 mIU/mL) and total anti-HBc negative. She completed the hepatitis B vaccine series. What is the best interpretation?

options.rationale: Correct. Anti-HBs without anti-HBc, after a completed series, is immunity inferred from vaccination.
Incorrect. Resolved infection would also show total anti-HBc, which every infection produces.
Incorrect. Chronic infection shows HBsAg and anti-HBc.
Incorrect. Susceptible persons are negative for anti-HBs as well.

questions.stem: A patient treated for primary syphilis had an RPR titer of 1:16 at treatment. Which follow-up result, using the same RPR method, shows a clinically significant decline?

options.rationale: Correct. 1:16 to 1:4 is a fourfold (two-dilution) fall, the threshold for a significant change.
Incorrect. A one-dilution change is within the test’s own variation.
Incorrect. Most treponemal tests stay reactive for life and are not used to judge treatment response.
Incorrect. RPR and VDRL titers cannot be compared directly; follow-up should use the same method.

questions.stem: A new lot of rapid antigen kits arrives. The built-in control line appears on every device tested. What should happen before patient testing with the new lot?

options.text: Run external positive and negative controls and confirm expected results
options.rationale: Correct. External controls check the whole process and are run with each new lot, each new shipment and each new tester.

options.text: Nothing; the built-in control proves the lot detects antigen
options.rationale: Incorrect. The built-in control shows the device ran with enough sample and correct flow; it does not check the whole process.

options.text: Calibrate the kit with patient samples
options.rationale: Incorrect. Quality control uses control materials of known reactivity, tested like patient samples; patient samples do not check the kit.
Incorrect. Both positive and negative reactivity should be checked.

accuracyFlags.issue: Anti-HBs positive with anti-HBc negative is immunity inferred from vaccination only with a vaccination history (≥10 mIU/mL after a completed series); anti-HBs within 6 months of HBIG is passive and does not show immune status.

CDC treats a fourfold (two-dilution) change in the same method as the threshold for a clinically significant difference, not as proof of cure; 10–20% of adequately treated people with primary or secondary syphilis do not achieve it, and criteria for cure are not well established. Treponemal tests stay reactive in the majority, not all, of patients.

The reviewer says internal control lines check flow only; CDC says built-in controls also show the test is working and the sample amount was adequate. External controls are due with each new shipment and each new tester as well as each new lot, and at least as often as the manufacturer specifies.
Control rules taught come from US sources (CDC waived-testing guidance; CLIA 42 CFR 493). Philippine regulatory requirements are not covered.
